The Crittenden Automotive Library: Bandidos Motorcycle Club, with an index of US Department of Justice releases
The Independent: Biker wars dredge up something rotten in the state of Denmark
CBC News: Timeline of the Bandidos massacre
CBC News: Search warrants reveal evidence in mass killing of 8 Bandidos members
CNN: Two biker gang leaders convicted for deadly 2015 shootout

NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth, Associated Press: Cases against bikers falter 3 years after Waco shootout

content.p: The Bandidos Motorcycle Club began in Texas in 1966 under the Vietnam War veteran Donald Chambers. It is now one of the best-known names in what police call outlaw motorcycle gangs, with chapters on several continents. Its name has turned up in three very different kinds of court record: a mass killing in an Ontario field, a parking-lot gunfight in Waco that produced almost 200 arrests and, three years on, no convictions, and a federal racketeering case that put its two top American officers in prison for life.

Club members quoted in the pages say they are bikers and not criminals. Law enforcement investigators quoted by CNN say clubs like it operate as criminal street gangs. Both claims run through the record below, and each is credited to the people who made it.

A page published by MCAC, a Maryland state site, says Donald Eugene Chambers founded the club in 1966 in San Leon, Texas. He was a Vietnam War veteran, and the page says he drew on his military life to build a culture of brotherhood and loyalty. The page says the name and the patch reflect a rebellious spirit against authority.

The patch shows a sombrero-wearing Mexican bandit with a pistol in one hand and a machete in the other. Members wear vests called "cuts" covered in patches that show allegiance and rank, and the club holds its meetings, which it calls "church", alongside regular group rides, MCAC says.

CNN describes the Bandidos as part of the "1%" outlaw biker world. It says investigators have long focused on such clubs because of that label, who say that 1% clubs, the Bandidos above all, operate as criminal street gangs and live "to instill fear and intimidation" in their rivals.

The MCAC page describes growth from Texas to chapters across the United States, Europe, Australia and Asia, and links the expansion to a wish for territory and influence that sometimes brought violent clashes with other clubs. The Crittenden library's index of Justice Department releases traces how the club later appeared in American enforcement actions: a September 2011 sweep that charged nearly 40 members and associates in three federal districts over alleged drug and firearms offences, and a 2023 task-force operation in New Mexico. In the second, the search warrant said officers in New Mexico, Texas and Oklahoma had seen a sharp rise in violence between the Bandidos and the Mongols club over four years.

One overseas conflict described in the pages consulted was in Scandinavia. The Independent reported in May 1996 that the Bandidos had first formed in Denmark in 1993, and that in the year before its report both the Bandidos and the Hells Angels had formed chapters in Norway, Sweden and Finland. A war between the two clubs had, the paper said, killed two people and wounded many in Sweden, Finland and Norway before it spread to Denmark about three weeks earlier. There, according to the paper, Bandidos members shot dead a Hells Angel returning from a convention in Helsinki outside the arrivals hall at Copenhagen airport. The gangs then fired rockets at each other's clubhouses, and a Bandidos leader, Morten Traeben, lost a leg when a grenade was thrown into his cell at an open prison. The Danish press, it added, reported that large stocks of weapons had been stolen from army stores in Denmark and Sweden.

The paper wrote that the Danish police were clearly caught off guard by the airport shooting. Morgens Sorenson, who headed Denmark's drugs intelligence unit, called the gangs an international organised-crime problem. A Bandidos spokesman who gave his name only as Jim told the reporter the club was "one big family", and said the drug accusations were untrue. Police, the paper said, estimated the gangs at about 50 strong, with supporters numbering in the thousands.

On 8 April 2006 a farmer and his wife saw three cars and a tow truck standing abandoned in an isolated field outside Shedden, about 30 kilometres south of London, Ontario. Police found the bodies of eight men inside the vehicles. CBC News reported that each was a Bandidos member or associate and each had been shot in the head. Search-warrant papers released in 2008 said blood-spatter evidence suggested some of the men were shot inside a vehicle while others were shot elsewhere and moved. The field lay a short distance from the home of Wayne Kellestine, and police sought to compare soil on a vehicle's wheels with soil on his farm.

The oldest victim was George Jesso, 52. John Muscedere, 48, was said to have been the club's Canadian president. The others were Francesco Salerno, 43, Luis Manny Raposo, 41, Jamie Flanz, 37, a prospective member, Michael Trotta, 31, an associate member, Paul Sinopoli, 30, and George Kriarakis, 28.

Five people were charged with first-degree murder in the days that followed. Murder charges against a common-law couple, Kerry Morris and Eric Niessen, were later replaced with accessory-after-the-fact charges, and in mid-June 2006 three men were arrested in Winnipeg, one of them a former police officer. Niessen pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice, admitting that he lied to police and helped Kellestine with a false alibi, and received two years in prison.

At the trial in Superior Court in London, Ontario, six men pleaded not guilty to eight counts of first-degree murder each. Over six months more than 70 witnesses testified. The Crown's star witness was a police informant identified only as M.H., a former Bandido. He told the court of tension between the club's Winnipeg group and its Toronto sponsor, which would not let the Manitoba group become a full chapter. M.H. testified that Michael Sandham had met United States club officials and returned saying the Toronto chapter "would be no more", and that the plan was for Kellestine to strip the Toronto members of their patches. According to M.H., the men spent hours before the meeting loading a cache of weapons to "be prepared for the worst". Kellestine's lawyer told the jury that Kellestine's farm had hosted the killings only because of the murderous intentions of a co-accused, Sandham, and described Kellestine as a madman who had turned a patch-stripping into murder. Sandham, a former police officer, told the court his reason for joining the gang was a wish to turn police informant. His evidence matched M.H.'s in many details but differed in others. M.H. said he saw Sandham shoot a victim.

The jury convicted all six. Kellestine, Sandham and Dwight Mushey were found guilty of eight counts of first-degree murder each. Frank Mather and Marcelo Aravena were each found guilty of seven counts of first-degree murder and one of manslaughter. Brett Gardiner was found guilty of six counts of first-degree murder and two of manslaughter. CBC noted that a first-degree murder conviction carries an automatic life sentence with no parole for 25 years, and described the case as believed to be Ontario's largest mass slaying.

On Sunday 17 May 2015, nine people were killed and about 20 were wounded at the Twin Peaks restaurant in Waco, Texas. The shooting capped a feud between the Bandidos and the Cossacks clubs. Investigators said it was triggered by rivalry ahead of a meeting. The bikers had come for a Confederation of Clubs gathering, a body that brings clubs together to talk about motorcycle matters. The Bandidos argue that the Cossacks were not part of it and had no reason to be there. The Cossacks say they came to make peace. Jake Carrizal, president of the Dallas Bandidos chapter, told CNN the Bandidos were "ambushed in a war zone"; Cossacks told CNN they came in peace and the Bandidos said they came in force to ambush them.

Waco police had been watching the gathering, and said officers opened fire after fights and gunfire broke out. The Associated Press wrote that ballistics evidence put police rounds in four of the nine dead, and in at least two cases the wounds were fatal. Authorities arrested nearly 200 people, and CNN counts 177 bikers charged in the roundup. McLennan County District Attorney Abel Reyna decided within hours to charge everyone with the same offence, engaging in organised criminal activity. Months later a grand jury indicted 154 bikers.

The strategy then unravelled. The AP reported that prosecutors had failed to convict a single person in three years. In the two weeks before the third anniversary, prosecutors dismissed 98 indictments and narrowed the cases to 25, three of them murder charges against Bandidos members Glenn Walker, Ray Allen and Jeff Battey. The AP said an agent had recovered one alleged murder weapon, Walker's pistol, from the back seat of a Waco SWAT car, where officers had tossed a pile of seized guns, and the agency could not match any fingerprints on it. Police records the AP had reviewed showed that a SWAT officer shot the Cossack Richard Kirschner twice, while the autopsy listed three gunshot wounds. In the death of another Cossack, Matthew Mark Smith, a firearms analysis could not tell which gun fired the fatal shot, and Allen's lawyer said Allen fired in self-defence.

The only case to reach a jury was that of Carrizal, who faced two counts of organised criminal activity and one of directing a criminal gang. His trial ended in a mistrial in November 2017 when the jury could not agree on any count. Carrizal told the jury "I am a Bandido. I'm not a criminal." Prosecutors presented evidence that he had a small handgun and fired it twice at a Cossack who had shot at him while he lay on the ground. He said he acted in self-defence. Reyna lost a Republican primary in March 2018 after accusations that he had mishandled the cases. Attorney Clint Broden, who represented three bikers, said the affair taught prosecutors to "investigate first and charge later". Around 130 bikers filed civil suits against the authorities, the AP reported.

His successor, Barry Johnson, took office in January 2019. In early April 2019 he said he was dismissing the 24 remaining cases, which were riot charges, a Class B misdemeanour carrying up to 180 days in jail. He said he lacked confidence that convictions would survive appeal and that further cases would waste public money. Nearly four years after the shooting, the lone Waco case to reach a jury had ended in a mistrial.
content.h2: The federal case against the leadership
content.p: A separate investigation, in which the FBI was already working with the Drug Enforcement Agency, was not part of the Waco inquiry, CNN reported. Fox reported that Pike was arrested in January 2016. On 17 May 2018 a federal jury in San Antonio convicted Jeffrey Pike, the national president from 2005 to 2016, and Xavier Portillo, the vice president, on 13 counts after a trial of nearly three months. The counts covered racketeering, drug trafficking, conspiracy to commit murder and extortion, CNN said.

Federal prosecutors alleged the two sanctioned years of violence against rival gangs to protect the "power, reputation and territory" of the Bandidos, and that Pike approved a declaration of war on the Cossacks that led to Twin Peaks. Pike told CNN he laughed when investigators asked him that, and said he had not committed a crime in decades. Fox News, citing the Associated Press, reported that the trial showed Portillo, with Pike's approval, waged a "war" on the Cossacks, and that jurors found Portillo took part in the 2002 killing of Robert Lara, and that Portillo and others trafficked methamphetamine and cocaine under an arrangement with the Texas Mexican Mafia.

The 2006 slaying of Anthony Benesh, who had been working to start a Texas chapter for the Hells Angels, set off the federal investigation, Fox reported. The Justice Department headlines listed by the Crittenden library, dated in September 2017, record that two, then a third and a fourth Bandido pleaded guilty to federal charges in connection with Benesh's murder. Headlines dated 24 and 26 September 2018 say the former national vice president and the former national president were sentenced to life in federal prison.

Court trouble has continued. On 19 February 2025 the Justice Department announced that an indictment had been unsealed in the Southern District of Texas charging 14 current and former members and associates of the Bandidos and the Mascareros Motorcycle Club with racketeering and murder. The release alleges a criminal enterprise engaged in murder, robbery, arson, drug distribution and witness intimidation in and around Houston. These are allegations in an indictment, and the pages consulted give no verdicts.
